opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think that's one of the more important uncertainties. The way I usually frame it is in terms of anchors. One anchor is: how much compute does the human brain use over a lifetime, roughly 10^24 FLOPs give or take, and how does that compare to what we'd need to train a model to do the same things? If ML were as sample-efficient as evolution-plus-development gives us, you'd expect transformative systems to be pretty cheap. But we have a lot of evidence that current methods are much less efficient than that: models see far more text than any human ever reads, and still have weird gaps.

So if you take seriously that we're three or four orders of magnitude worse, a few things follow. First, it pushes the compute requirement up, but three or four orders of magnitude isn't actually that much on the scales we're talking about. Spending has been growing fast, hardware keeps improving, and algorithmic progress has been chipping away at efficiency at something like an order of magnitude every few years. So a gap of that size might cost you maybe a decade or so, not a century.

Second, I don't think the gap is fixed. Part of the inefficiency is that we're training from scratch on a narrow data distribution, while the brain comes with a lot of evolutionary prior built in. Some of that we can substitute for with more data and compute, and some of it we'll recover through better algorithms. The question is less "will we ever match the brain" and more "how much overhead do you pay at the point where systems become economically transformative?"

Third, and I think this gets underweighted, you don't need to match human efficiency across the board. You need systems useful enough to accelerate R&D, including AI research itself. A system that's a thousand times less sample-efficient than a human can still be extremely valuable if you can run huge numbers of copies, run them fast, and give them more experience than any person gets in a lifetime. Once you're in that regime, the efficiency gap starts closing faster, because the systems help close it.

So my practical take: it's a real reason not to expect transformative AI to be trivially easy, and it widens the error bars. But it doesn't push me toward very long timelines. It moves the median a bit later and fattens the tail, and I'd still put substantial probability on things getting very wild within the next couple of decades.

r001.rationale: The response says the efficiency gap might add only about a decade, does not push toward very long timelines, and still assigns substantial probability to major changes within a couple of decades.

r002.rationale: It gives the brain's lifetime compute as roughly 10^24 FLOPs and says the inefficiency raises compute needs, but never estimates AI training compute at roughly 10^27.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think that observation is real, and it's one of the main things that makes me uncertain about timelines in both directions. If you look at how much data a human sees over a lifetime, it's something like a billion tokens, give or take, and current models are trained on trillions of tokens to reach roughly comparable performance on a lot of tasks. So on a naive sample-efficiency comparison, we're off by several orders of magnitude.

The question is what that gap means. There are a few interpretations, and I put real weight on more than one.

One interpretation is that evolution did a lot of the work. The human brain isn't a blank slate trained on a billion tokens; it's a blank slate plus an architecture and a bunch of inductive biases that were selected over hundreds of millions of years. So you could say the fair comparison includes that search, and then the total compute looks much larger and the gap shrinks a lot. On that view, the inefficiency of ML is mostly that we're doing the evolutionary search ourselves, by gradient descent and by researchers trying things, rather than having it handed to us. That doesn't make me think timelines are long, it just reframes where the cost is.

A second interpretation is that our algorithms are genuinely bad and there's a lot of low-hanging algorithmic improvement left. If that's right, you'd expect progress to be lumpy and faster than the pure compute-scaling story predicts, because somebody finds something that closes a chunk of that gap and suddenly you're three orders of magnitude further along. That's the version that should make people nervous about short timelines, because it means scaling trends understate what's possible.

A third interpretation, which I think people underweight, is that the comparison is just confused. Humans and models are learning different things from different data. A child gets an enormous amount of grounded, interactive, multimodal experience, with feedback loops, with the ability to act and see consequences. A language model gets text. It's not obvious the token counts are measuring the same thing, and part of what looks like inefficiency may be the model having to reconstruct a lot of structure from a much more impoverished signal.

Where I come out is roughly this. I think the sample-efficiency gap is one of the reasons I don't fully trust extrapolations that say "just keep scaling compute at the current rate and you get there by year X." It cuts both ways. It means we might be further than the loss curves suggest, because there's slack in the algorithms. But it also means that if that slack never gets closed, pure scaling could hit a wall where the data you'd need just doesn't exist, and then you're relying on synthetic data or RL or something else to make up the difference.

So I don't treat it as a strong argument for long timelines. If anything, I treat it as a source of variance. My median hasn't moved that much because of it, but my tails have gotten fatter. I think the most likely resolution is that over the next decade we close a meaningful fraction of the gap, maybe one or two orders of magnitude, through a combination of architectural changes and better use of data, and that this ends up being a significant input into when we get systems that can do most of what humans do, rather than a thing that stalls it.

r001.rationale: The candidate says algorithmic improvements could make short timelines more concerning, but concludes the efficiency gap is mainly a source of variance and has not moved their median timeline much. It does not clearly interpret the gap as favoring shorter timelines.

r002.rationale: The candidate gives no estimate of a 10^27 training-compute requirement.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s evidence that there’s a lot of room for algorithmic improvement, but it doesn’t by itself tell you how soon that improvement will happen. And I’d want to distinguish a few meanings of efficiency. Are we talking about how much data you need, how much computation you need to learn from that data, or how much energy you use? Those can give you pretty different answers.

If you mean that humans learn from much less experience, that seems like a significant observation. But humans also come into the world with a lot of structure supplied by evolution. It’s hard to know how much of the difference is a better general-purpose learning algorithm and how much is having the right prior for the kinds of tasks we’re looking at.

For timelines, I’d think about two routes. One is that we keep using relatively inefficient algorithms and compensate with more compute. The other is that we find algorithms that close some of that gap. You don’t need to close the entire gap for the second route to matter a lot.

So I wouldn’t take the observation as a straightforward argument for long timelines. It could mean current approaches are going to be expensive to scale. But it also means there’s potentially a large amount of progress available without increasing compute. The important question is how hard those improvements are to discover, and the comparison with the brain doesn’t settle that.

r001.rationale: The response says the efficiency gap does not settle timelines and is not a straightforward argument for long timelines; it does not clearly interpret the gap as favoring shorter timelines.

r002.rationale: The response gives no estimate of a training-compute requirement near 10^27.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to be careful about what you mean by efficiency there. You could mean how much experience you need to learn something, or you could mean how much computation you need to turn that experience into a useful capability. Those have pretty different implications for timelines.

If the claim is that there are algorithms that use a thousand or ten thousand times less computation than our current algorithms, then that’s potentially a reason AI could arrive much sooner than you’d predict by extrapolating hardware. But it doesn’t tell you when we’ll discover those algorithms. You could believe there’s a lot of room for improvement and still think getting there will take a long time.

I’m also hesitant to make the comparison directly from how much data a person sees. A human comes into the world with a lot of structure supplied by evolution. We don’t know how much of the apparent advantage is coming from that structure, how much is coming from better learning algorithms, and how much is because we’re comparing different tasks.

So I would mostly treat this as uncertainty about how much algorithmic progress is possible. I wouldn’t take a particular estimate of the gap and mechanically move my timeline forward or backward by that amount.

r001.rationale: The response says that if the efficiency gap means current algorithms need far more computation, that could make AI arrive sooner than hardware extrapolation would suggest.

r002.rationale: The response gives no estimate of a training-compute requirement around 10^27.
